results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. Creatures that phase in do not trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing is a static ability that makes certain permanents phase out and in during the untap step (they change to “phased out” or “phased in” without changing zones) [702.26a]. When a permanent phases in, it simply becomes phased in and the game treats it as though it exists again [702.26c]. However, phasing is not a zone change, and zone-change triggers (including enters-the-battlefield abilities) don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out [702.26d; 603.6a]. The phasing action that causes permanents to phase in and out during the untap step happens as a turn-based action and doesn’t use the stack [502.1], so you don’t get normal ETB trigger timing from that action. Assumption: this answer covers all normal ways a permanent “phases in” (including the untap step); if an effect instead moves a permanent into the battlefield from another zone, that is a zone change and would trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities per the usual rules [603.6a].

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Direct answer: When a creature with both trample and deathtouch assigns combat damage, you may assign only 1 damage to each blocking creature (that 1 is treated as lethal because of deathtouch) and assign the rest as excess damage to the defending player or planeswalker, subject to the usual trample rules about checking already-marked damage and multiple blockers. After damage is dealt, creatures dealt damage by a source with deathtouch are destroyed by state-based actions.

Definitions
- Trample: a static ability that changes how an attacking creature assigns combat damage; it applies only while the creature is attacking (see rule 702.19a and 702.19b). When assigning, you must assign lethal damage to blocking creatures first, then may assign any excess among those blockers and the player/planeswalker being attacked (702.19b).
- Deathtouch: a keyword that makes any nonzero amount of damage from that source count as lethal damage for assignment purposes; a creature dealt damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action (702.2c, 702.2b, 704.5h).

How they interact (step-by-step, assignment then result)
1) Damage assignment: During the combat damage assignment step you follow the trample assignment rules (510.1, 702.19b). When determining how much is "lethal" to a blocking creature, deathtouch makes any nonzero damage from that source lethal (702.2c). Also take into account damage already marked on the blocking creature and damage being assigned at the same time from other creatures (702.19b; 120.6). Concretely, a trampling creature that has deathtouch need only assign 1 point of damage to each blocking creature to meet the requirement to assign lethal damage to that creature; any remaining power can be assigned as excess to the defending player or planeswalker as allowed by trample (120.4a, 702.19b).
2) Damage dealing and aftermath: When damage is actually dealt, the deathtouch damage will cause the damaged blocking creatures to be destroyed by state-based actions (702.2b; 704.5h). Note that trample only affected how you assigned the damage; destruction happens afterward via state-based actions.

Short example (assumption: two-player or multiplayer alike — the result is the same): A 6/6 attacking creature with trample and deathtouch is blocked by a 3/3. When assigning damage you may assign 1 damage to the 3/3 (that 1 is lethal because of deathtouch) and assign the other 5 damage to the defending player. After damage is dealt the 3/3 will be destroyed by state-based actions.

Assumptions and timing note: I assumed the normal order where assignment happens in the combat damage assignment step, then damage is dealt, then state-based actions are checked. If damage was already marked on blockers or other creatures were assigning damage simultaneously, that affects how much must be assigned to reach "lethal" (see 702.19b and 120.6).

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes. “Storm” is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, and that triggered ability can be countered — but only by effects that specifically counter abilities, not by effects that only counter spells. Reasoning: “Storm” is defined as a triggered ability that creates copies when you cast the spell and functions on the stack [702.40a]. A triggered ability is an ability with a trigger condition and an effect [603.1a], and when its trigger event occurs the ability is put on the stack as an object the next time a player would receive priority [603.2a, 603.3]. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells and therefore can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells; they can, however, be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9]. (Multiple storm instances trigger separately [702.40b].)

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No — a card with a hybrid mana symbol is considered to have every color shown in that symbol in its color identity, so you may only include that card in a commander deck if every color in the hybrid symbol is already in your commander’s color identity. For example, a card with {R/G} in its mana cost has both red and green in its color identity, so it can’t go in a strictly mono-red commander deck (the commander must have both red and green to allow that card).

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No — you cannot respond during the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so spells can’t be cast and activated abilities can’t be activated or resolve during that step [502.4]. The untap action itself is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack (the active player determines which permanents will untap, then they untap simultaneously) [502.3], and priority (the ability to cast spells or activate abilities) is what allows players to take those actions [117.1]. Any abilities that trigger as the untap step happens are held and then put onto the stack at the beginning of the upkeep before the active player gets priority, so you can respond once the upkeep begins and those triggered abilities are on the stack [502.4] [503.1a] [117.3a].

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text:
Yes. Creatures are still attacking creatures during the end of combat step. 

Definition: "Attacking Creature." A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase or was put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first [Attacking Creature].

Reasoning: Creatures remain attacking through the end of combat step because they stop being attacking only when they are removed from combat or when the combat phase ends [Attacking Creature]; rule 508.4d reiterates that such creatures remain attacking until removed from combat or the combat phase ends. "At end of combat" triggered abilities trigger as the end of combat step begins, and effects that last "until end of combat" do not expire at the start of the end of combat step but instead expire when the combat phase ends (i.e., when the end of combat step ends) [511.2; 500.5a]. As soon as the end of combat step ends, all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat and the combat phase is over, after which the postcombat main phase begins [511.3].

Exception/related note: If an effect ends the combat phase (for example, Mandate of Peace), the end of combat step may be skipped and "at end of combat" triggered abilities won’t trigger in that case [724.2e]. Also, a permanent is removed from combat for any of the listed reasons in rule 506.4 (for example, if it leaves the battlefield or its controller changes) [506.4].

Assumptions: I assume a normal turn sequence where the end of combat step is not skipped by a special effect; the conclusion is the same in multiplayer and two-player games under these rules.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No — you do not cast lands. Lands are played as a special action (you “play a land”), not cast as spells.

Definitions
- “To play a land”: to put a land onto the battlefield from the zone it’s in (usually your hand). This is a special action that you may take only when you have priority during a main phase of your turn, the stack is empty, and you haven’t played a land this turn; playing a land doesn’t use the stack and the land is never a spell (so it can’t be countered and players can’t respond to the act of playing it). [701.18a] [305.1] [116.2a] [505.6b] [305.2b]
- “To cast” (brief): to play a card as a spell (i.e., the alternative to playing a card as a land). See the play/cast wording. [601.1a] [701.18b]

Additional points you should know
- Lands normally have no mana cost and are played without paying costs. [202.1b]
- An effect that simply “puts” a land onto the battlefield is not the same as playing a land and does not count toward your one-land-per-turn limit. [305.4]
- An object that’s both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. [300.2a] [305.9]
- You can’t play a land if it isn’t your turn. Ignore any instruction that would let you play a land on someone else’s turn. [305.3]

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes. “Loses all abilities” includes keyword abilities — keywords are abilities, and an effect that makes an object lose abilities removes those keyword abilities.

Definition: A keyword ability is a named ability listed as a keyword on an object (for example, “flying”); an object described as “with [keyword ability]” or “that has [keyword ability]” is merely said to have that ability ([702.1], [702.1d]).

Why: Effects that remove abilities make the object “lose” those abilities (they remove abilities from the object) ([113.10]). When continuous effects that add or remove abilities are applied, they’re handled in the ability layer (Layer 6), which governs ability-adding and ability-removing effects together ([613.1f]). Because keyword abilities are abilities, they are subject to those ability-removing effects (see the explicit example that if an effect causes a permanent to lose banding, it loses all “bands with other” abilities as well) ([702.22b]).

Clarification: Abilities are different from characteristic-defining effects or effects that simply state a quality (for example, “is red” or “can’t be blocked” when those are worded as set qualities); losing abilities doesn’t affect characteristics set by non-ability continuous effects ([113.12]).

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text:
Yes. A player may draw cards even if that player already has as many cards as their maximum hand size; the maximum hand size only forces discards during the cleanup step, it does not prevent drawing.

Why: "Maximum hand size" means how many cards a player may keep at the end of their cleanup step (normally seven) — players may have any number of cards in hand at other times and must discard down to the maximum during the cleanup step [402.2, 514.1, 703.4n]. The rules about drawing show that drawing is an action that can occur and is not blocked merely because a player already has the maximum number of cards [121.2, 121.3]. (If an effect uses different wording — for example, it moves cards from library to hand without using the word "draw" — that is not a draw for purposes of replacement effects or draw-restrictions [121.5].)

Assumptions and special cases: I assume there is no other effect saying that the player "can't draw cards." If such an effect exists, it would prevent draws or prevent the choice to draw as described by those effects [121.3, 121.3a]. Also, if drawing (or being required to draw) would attempt to draw more cards than remain in the player's library, different rules apply: the player draws as many as possible and then may lose the game as described by the rules on running out of library cards [609.3, 104.3c]. Replacement effects that replace draws still apply even if no cards could be drawn because the library is empty [121.6, 614.11].

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text:
No — a non-creature artifact does not “die.”

Definition and ruling: The term dies applies only to a creature or a planeswalker: “A creature or planeswalker ‘dies’ if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.” [Dies] [700.4]. A non-creature artifact is a noncreature permanent, and the word dies does not apply to it. If a non‑creature artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, it is not considered to have died. Note also that a permanent can be “destroyed” by an effect that uses the word “destroy” (or by certain state-based actions); that still isn’t the same as the term dies, which is limited to creatures and planeswalkers. [701.8b]

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
You lose the game the next time a player would receive priority if you attempt to draw a card and your library has no cards in it. This applies to turn-based draws (such as the draw step) and to effects that use the word “draw.”

Explanation and important details:
- Draw = putting the top card of your library into your hand (rule 121.1; Draw). An ordinary draw from an empty library counts as an attempt to draw from a library with no cards, which causes you to lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (rules 121.4 and 704.5b). State-based actions are the mechanism that enforces that loss (704.1). 
- If an effect requires you to draw more cards than remain in your library, you draw whatever cards remain and then you lose the next time a player would receive priority (104.3c). Apply “do as much as possible” when an effect tries to move more cards than exist (609.3). 
- Replacement effects that replace draws are applied even if no cards could be drawn because your library is empty (121.6a; 614.11). If an effect moves cards from the library to your hand without using the word “draw,” those moves are not draws and therefore do not by themselves trigger the “draw from empty library” loss rule (121.5). 
- If an effect merely offers you the choice to draw and your library is empty, you may choose to take that choice (121.3 and 121.3a); choosing to do so is an attempt to draw and will produce the same loss outcome described above.

Assumptions: This answer uses the provided rules only and assumes the usual game context (two-player or multiplayer—this outcome is the same regardless of player count). If a specific replacement effect or card interaction is involved, that card’s text or rulings could change the result; the provided rules require applying any replacement effect that applies to the draw even when the library is empty (121.6a; 614.11).

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
Direct answer: The combat phase has five steps — beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat — and several of those steps contain turn‑based actions that do not use the stack, so you don’t get priority to cast spells or activate abilities during those turn‑based actions. The provided rules do not contain the full rule that tells exactly who gets priority at each moment between those steps, so I can’t state every instant when the defending player will have priority from the given text; see “What’s missing” below.

Definitions
- Priority: The player who currently has priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions [117.1].
- Turn‑based action: A required action that happens at a particular moment in a step and “does not use the stack” (so players don’t get to cast spells/activate abilities while that action is being performed) — several combat actions are turn‑based actions in the rules below (see citations).

What the rules you gave say (step list and what happens in each):
1) Beginning of combat step — part of the combat phase. In multiplayer games in which the active player’s opponents don’t all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player as a turn‑based action immediately after the beginning of combat step begins; that turn‑based action doesn’t use the stack [506.1][506.2a][507.1][703.4h]. (If the “all opponents are defending” multiplayer option is in effect, instead all opponents are defending players during the combat phase [802.2].)

2) Declare attackers step — listed as the second step of combat [506.1]. (The provided excerpt doesn’t add more about priority here.)

3) Declare blockers step — when it begins, the defending player declares blockers; that is a turn‑based action that doesn’t use the stack [506.1][509.1][703.4j]. If no creatures were declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped [506.1].

4) Combat damage step — first each player in APNAP order announces how each attacking or blocking creature they control assigns its combat damage (this is a turn‑based action that doesn’t use the stack); specifically, the active player announces how each attacking creature assigns, then the defending player announces how each blocking creature assigns [703.4k][510.1][802.5]. After assignment, all combat damage that’s been assigned is dealt simultaneously; that damage dealing is a turn‑based action and no player has a chance to cast spells or activate abilities between assignment and dealing [510.2]. (There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].)

5) End of combat step — the end of combat step has no turn‑based actions; once it begins, the active player gets priority [511.1].

In other words, you do not have priority to take those stack actions while those turn‑based actions themselves are being performed. Also, after combat damage is assigned and before it’s dealt there is no chance to cast spells or activate abilities [510.2].
- Outside those listed turn‑based actions, who actually has priority at each moment is governed by the general priority system [117.1], but the excerpt you provided does not include the rule text that specifies precisely which player receives priority at each point between steps. Because that specific rule text isn’t in the provided context, I can’t enumerate every exact instant when the defending player will be the player with priority.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:
No — you can’t “respond” to a mana ability. A mana ability doesn’t use the stack and resolves immediately when it’s activated, so nothing can be cast or activated in response to it.

Definitions and key points
- “Mana ability”: an activated ability is a mana ability if it (a) doesn’t require a target, (b) could add mana to a player’s mana pool when it resolves, and (c) isn’t a loyalty ability [605.1a]. Mana abilities are a subset of the things called out in rule 113.4.
- “Respond”: to cast an instant or activate an ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack (see rule 117.7). Because mana abilities don’t go on the stack, you can’t respond to them in that sense [117.7, 605.3b].

Why you can’t respond
- Activating a mana ability is governed by special exceptions: mana abilities don’t go on the stack and thus can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to; they resolve immediately after being activated [605.3b, 405.6c].
- Triggered mana abilities likewise resolve immediately when they trigger (they don’t wait for priority) and so can’t be responded to either [605.4a].
- Once a player begins to activate a mana ability, that same ability can’t be activated again until it resolves [605.3c].

What this doesn’t stop
- An ability that has a target is not a mana ability (even if it could put mana into a player’s pool) and follows normal activated/triggered-ability rules, so such an ability can be put on the stack and can be responded to [605.5a].
- You may still activate mana abilities whenever the rules allow (for example, whenever you have priority or when a rule asks you to pay mana), but those activations themselves aren’t things other players can respond to with spells or abilities on the stack [117.1d, 605.3a].

This is the same in multiplayer and two-player games: mana abilities never use the stack, so they can’t be responded to in either case.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Direct answer: "Layers" are the system the game uses to determine the exact order in which continuous effects are applied to an object; you start with the object’s printed characteristics and then apply continuous effects in the layers in the order the rules give. Continuous effects are applied continually and instantaneously, and effects that modify different kinds of characteristics are applied in different numbered layers and (when relevant) sublayers and timestamp/dependency order.

How it works, step by step (grounded in the provided rules):
- Start with the object’s actual values (for a card, the printed values) as the baseline [613.1].
- Continuous effects are applied in a fixed series of layers; the rules call this the Layer system and list the layers used to order those effects [Layer], [613.1]. Examples of layers named in the provided text include Layer 1 (rules/effects that modify copiable values) [613.1a], Layer 3 (text-changing effects) [613.1c], Layer 4 (type-changing effects) [613.1d], Layer 5 (color-changing effects) [613.1e], and Layer 7 (power/toughness effects) [613.1], with layer 7 further broken into sublayers [613.4].
- Within a layer or sublayer, effects are generally applied in timestamp order (earlier timestamps first) [613.7]. Some layers are explicitly applied in a series of sublayers in a particular order, and within each sublayer timestamp order is used [613.2], [613.2a], [613.4].
- Dependency can override timestamp order when one effect depends on the existence or result of another; in that case the dependency system determines the order instead of timestamps [Dependency], [613.8].
- If a single effect has parts that apply in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer, and once that multi-part effect begins applying it continues to apply to the same set of objects across those layers even if the source of the effect is removed during the process [613.6].
- Continuous effects are applied continually and instantaneously by the game; the layer application is not a one-time calculation but the game’s ongoing method of determining current characteristics [613.5].

Illustrative examples from the rules text (showing how layers change results):
- Honor of the Pure and a 2/2 black creature: if an effect later turns that creature white (a color change, layer 5), the creature becomes affected by Honor of the Pure’s bonus (applied in the appropriate power/toughness layer) and changes size accordingly; if the creature’s color later changes to red (layer 5), Honor of the Pure stops applying [613.5].
- A scenario with counters, a spell that sets or grants +X/+X, and an effect that sets power/toughness to specific values shows how layer 7 sublayers interact so the final power/toughness is the result of applying those sublayers in order and by timestamps/dependency where needed [613.5].
- Act of Treason’s example shows a single effect that is both a control-changing effect (layer 2) and an ability-adding effect (layer 6); the gain-control part is applied in layer 2 and the haste-granting part in layer 6 [613.6].
- Svogthos, the Restless Tomb’s example shows type-changing effects (layer 4) and power/toughness-setting effects (layer 7b) both applying to the same permanent, and how later changes to the graveyard can alter the power/toughness because the power/toughness-setting part keeps applying in layer 7b [613.6].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text:
Direct answer: When a player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the exact same name, that player chooses one of them to keep and all the others are put into their owners’ graveyards as a state-based action. This effect is called the legend rule and is applied automatically (no player gets priority to respond to it). 

Explanation and key definitions:
- “Legend rule” (the rule being applied) is the state-based action that causes a player who controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name to choose one and put the rest into their owners’ graveyards. See rule [704.5j].
- “Legendary” is a supertype. Any permanent with the supertype “legendary” is subject to the legend rule. See rules [Legendary] and [205.4d].
- A token that is created with a specific name and the legendary supertype (for example, an instruction reading “create [name], a . . .” that gives it the legendary supertype) is a legendary permanent with that name and is therefore subject to the legend rule. See rule [111.9].
- Objects that gained or lost other card types or subtypes but remain legendary are still legendary because supertypes are independent; changing an object’s other types doesn’t remove the legendary supertype. See rule [205.4b].
- Planeswalker cards printed before the planeswalker-uniqueness rule was removed were given the legendary supertype and are therefore subject to the legend rule like any other legendary permanent. See rule [306.4].

Assumptions and scope: I’m describing how the legend rule operates on legendary permanents on the battlefield (the usual application). If you meant a different situation (for example, how legendary spells are cast from the stack), note that legendary instants and sorceries have a separate casting restriction; that casting restriction is not the legend rule itself (see [205.4e]). This answer applies the same way in multiplayer as in two-player games—the rule is checked for each player’s controlled permanents separately. 

Practical note: the rule uses “owners’ graveyards,” so the cards put into graveyards go to their owners rather than necessarily to the controller who had them on the battlefield. See [704.5j].

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature is destroyed as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked after the damage is dealt — in practice, immediately after that damage is processed and before any player receives priority. 

Definition (key term). "Lethal damage" means an amount of damage marked on a creature greater than or equal to that creature’s toughness (so damage marked ≥ toughness is lethal). [704.5g][120.6]

Why and when this happens, step by step: 
- Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect is marked on that creature. [120.3e]
- After damage is dealt, it is processed into its results. [120.4c] 
- The game performs state-based actions automatically and without using the stack; state-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority (and at other specific times). [704.1][117.5][117.2d]
- One state-based action is: if a creature with toughness greater than 0 has damage marked on it that is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed. Regeneration can replace that destruction event. [704.5g]
- Therefore, once the damage is processed and the creature has damage marked ≥ its toughness, the creature is destroyed as the next state-based-action check (i.e., immediately, before anyone gets priority). [120.4c][704.5g][117.5]

Other practical notes and assumptions: 
- Damage marked on a permanent remains until it’s removed by regeneration or the cleanup step; marking lethal damage doesn’t itself remove the damage. [120.6][514.2]
- Damage itself doesn’t "destroy" the creature directly; the destruction comes from the state-based action. [120.5]
- If this is combat damage, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously, then processed and state-based actions are checked immediately afterward. In that case the destruction happens at that same immediate SBA check. [703.4m][120.4c][704.5g]

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text:
No — you can’t simply cast your commander from exile unless a rule or effect explicitly lets you cast cards from exile. To “cast” means to take the card from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs (the steps in rule 601.2b and 601.2f); you can begin that process only if a rule or effect allows you to cast the card (rule 601.3f). The Commander-specific rule that normally lets you cast a commander (rule 903.8) applies only to casting it from the command zone, not from exile.

Also note two interactions that commonly matter here: (1) If your commander was put into exile just now, rule 903.9a says that as a state-based action its owner may put that commander into the command zone instead (see rule 704.1 for state-based actions). If the owner does that, the owner may then cast the commander from the command zone under rule 903.8 (paying any commander tax). (2) Certain card-specific rules allow casting particular cards from exile (for example, a plotted card may be cast from exile under rule 702.170d, and an Adventure card exiled by its Adventure ability may be played from exile under rule 715.3d); you can cast a commander from exile only if an effect like those explicitly authorizes it. Also be aware some replacement effects can instead redirect a card that would be put into exile to the command zone (for example, the Astrotorium-card-back replacement in rule 717.6).

Assumptions: I assume no other effect is granting permission to cast cards from exile in your situation. If a face-down exile is involved, rule 406.3b adds the extra requirement that you must be allowed to look at the face-down exiled card before you may cast it under any effect that permits casting face-down exiled cards.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
Direct answer — what happens in the cleanup step: It is the second and final step of the ending phase during which a specific set of turn-based actions happen (and normally no player has priority). In order:

1) Discard to maximum hand size: First, if the active player’s hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size, that player discards enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. This discard is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack (see rules [514.1] and [703.4n]).

2) Remove damage and end “until end of turn” effects: Immediately after that discard action, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. This happens simultaneously and doesn’t use the stack (see rules [514.2] and [703.4p]). Note that damage stays on creatures until this cleanup removal (see rule [120.6]).

3) Expire end-of-step effects and empty mana pools: Any effects that last until the end of that step or phase expire, then any unspent mana in players’ mana pools empties (this is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack) (see rule [500.5]).

4) Priority and triggered abilities: Normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so spells can’t be cast and abilities can’t be activated (see rule [514.3]). The exception is: if state-based actions would be performed and/or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including abilities that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), then the game performs the state-based actions, those triggered abilities are put onto the stack, and then the active player gets priority (see rule [514.3a]). After those triggers resolve (each resolves when all players pass in succession), if the stack becomes empty and players pass, another cleanup step begins (see rules [608.1] and [704.3]). If on the first check during the cleanup step no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, then no player gets priority and the cleanup step ends (see rule [704.3]).

5) Interactions with “end the turn” effects: If an effect ends the turn, the game skips straight to the cleanup step; if an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins. During the process of ending the turn no player gets priority, and any triggered abilities that have triggered since that process began are put onto the stack during the cleanup step as described above (see rules [724.1d] and [724.1f]).

Assumptions and scope: This answer is based only on the provided rules text; no card-specific oracle text or table-specific multiplayer exceptions beyond those included were assumed. The description applies the same way whether the game is two-player or multiplayer under the provided rules (no multiplayer-specific difference is given in the supplied rules).

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked automatically any time the game would give a player priority: the game checks for and performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event, repeats that check until no state-based actions are performed, and only then gives priority. (This also happens during the cleanup step’s special-case check described below.)

Definition: A state-based action is a game action that happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met; state-based actions don’t use the stack. [704.1]

When and how they’re checked (summary of the timing rules):
- They’re checked throughout the game whenever a player would get priority. The game performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event, repeats the check if any were performed, and only when no more are performed do triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack get put on the stack and the player receives priority. [704.3] [117.5]
- Turn-based actions that occur when a step or phase begins are handled first; after those are dealt with, state-based actions are checked before the player receives priority. [703.3] [117.3a]
- Normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, but there’s an exception: if a cleanup-step check finds that any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, the state-based actions are performed, those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. [514.3a]
- State-based actions are game actions checked throughout the game (not actions a player chooses to take). [704.2] [704.1]

Assumption: I assume a normal two-player game; the provided rules apply as written and cover the relevant multiplayer differences only insofar as they appear in these rules. If you want examples of specific state-based actions or how they interact with spell resolution timing, say which situation you have in mind.

results.question: when can I concede a game?

Additional points you can act on:

- Conceding is an action that doesn’t use the stack and can be done at any time (see [405.6g]).

Direct answer: The active player is the player whose turn it is. See rule [102.1].

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
Direct answer: The player who cast the spell (even if they aren’t the active player) gets priority immediately after casting that spell.

Definition: “Priority” is the game state that allows a player to cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions [117.1].

Why: Rule 117.3c says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward, so a nonactive player who casts a spell keeps priority right after casting it [117.3c]. If that spell was cast while another spell or ability was already on the stack, the newly cast spell is considered cast “in response to” the earlier one and will resolve first (the new spell resolves before the earlier one) [117.7]. (After spells or abilities resolve, the active player normally receives priority [117.3b].)

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text:
Yes — as long as you had priority when you began casting a spell, you receive priority afterward and may cast additional spells. Priority is the game state that lets a player cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions [117.1]. The rules state explicitly that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward [117.3c]; rule 601.2i repeats that if the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority. That lets you cast more spells “in response” to things already on the stack; a spell you cast while another object is on the stack is cast in response and will resolve first [117.7].

Exceptions and related notes (assumptions stated):
- If an effect allows you to cast a spell during the resolution of something, follow the casting steps but no player receives priority after that cast, so you do not get to keep priority in that case [608.2g].
- During the cleanup step, players normally don’t receive priority, so you can’t cast spells then unless some effect changes that [514.3].
- In team games, teams (not individual players) have priority, so the team-level priority rules govern who may act [805.5a]. In Grand Melee games with multiple stacks, you must specify which stack you’re putting a cast spell on when you cast while you control priority for multiple stacks [807.5b].
- If you attempt an illegal cast, the action is reversed and the player who had priority retains it and may redo a legal action or do something else [733.1, 733.2].
- A phase or step doesn’t end until the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, so you (or anyone who currently has priority) can keep adding spells while that condition isn’t met [500.2].

Assumption: I assumed you had priority before you began casting (the rules that let you “keep” priority apply only in that case). If you did not have priority when the cast began (for example, the spell was cast as part of resolution where no one receives priority afterward), the ‘‘keep priority’’ statements above don’t apply [601.2i, 608.2g].

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?

Lore counters are put on Sagas in two ways: (1) as the Saga enters the battlefield (it “enters with” lore counter(s) because each Saga has an intrinsic replacement ability), and (2) thereafter as a turn‑based action immediately after the active player’s precombat main phase begins (the active player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities). Definitions and supporting detail: a “Saga” is an enchantment card with chapter symbols in its text box and “Sagas use lore counters to track their progress” (a Saga’s chapter abilities look for lore counters being put on it) [714.1; 714.3]. A Saga without read ahead has the intrinsic replacement ability “This Saga enters with a lore counter on it” [714.3a], while a Saga with read ahead has the intrinsic replacement abilities that let its controller choose a number between one and its final chapter number and make it enter with that many lore counters [714.3b; 702.155a; 702.155b]. Replacement effects that read “enters with” or “as [this permanent] enters” apply as the permanent enters [614.1c]. The turn‑based action that puts lore counters on Sagas happens immediately after the active player’s precombat main phase begins and doesn’t use the stack (this is performed by the active player for Sagas they control) [703.4f; 714.3c; 505.4].
