results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect as a spell or ability resolves (or when a replacement or certain static effects are applied) that waits and then triggers later, typically containing “when,” “whenever,” or “at.” [603.7] It’s created during resolution (or when a replacement or static ability applies) and won’t trigger until after it has actually been created; if the thing it would watch for already happened before creation, it won’t trigger for that earlier event. [603.7a] A delayed triggered ability normally triggers only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration (for example, “this turn”). If the trigger event would occur more than once simultaneously and there’s no stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes it to trigger. [603.7b] If the delayed triggered ability refers to a particular object, it still affects that object even if the object’s characteristics change, but it does nothing if the object is no longer in the zone the ability expects it to be in when the ability tries to affect it (and if the object left and returned it’s a new object and won’t be affected). [603.7c] Delayed triggered abilities can be created by spells, activated or triggered abilities, replacement effects, or static abilities that allow or instruct a player to take an action; the source and controller of the delayed triggered ability depend on what created it (for a spell, the spell is the source and its controller is the ability’s controller; for an activated/triggered ability, the other ability is the source and its controller is the delayed ability’s controller; when a static ability’s replacement effect creates one, the object with that static ability is the source and its controller at that time is the delayed ability’s controller; likewise for static abilities that allow a player to take an action). [603.7d] [603.7e] [603.7f] [603.7g] Some one‑shot effects create delayed triggered abilities as part of their resolution. [610.2] If a delayed triggered ability refers to an X from the spell or ability that created it, X has the same value for the delayed triggered ability as it did for the creating spell or ability. [107.3n] A permanent being put onto the battlefield by a resolving permanent spell can create a delayed triggered ability as it enters. [608.3g] Reflexive triggered abilities are a special case of delayed triggered abilities that are checked immediately after creation to see whether the earlier part of the resolution produced the event they look for; if so, they trigger then. [603.12]

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes. By “non‑permanent spells” I assume you mean instant and sorcery spells on the stack; those objects can have abilities. Any text on an instant or sorcery is a spell ability unless that text is instead an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that meets the exception in rule 113.6 [113.3a]. Spell abilities are followed as instructions while the instant or sorcery spell is resolving, and abilities of an instant or sorcery usually function only while that object is on the stack [113.3a, 113.6]. An instant or sorcery can also have activated or triggered abilities; those are abilities on the stack when they’re activated or triggered (they’re not spells) and are treated as abilities rather than as spells while on the stack [113.1c, 113.9]. Static abilities normally function on the battlefield, though rule 113.6 describes exceptions for instants or sorceries. When an instant or sorcery resolves, it may create one‑shot or continuous effects as a result of its abilities [609.1]. Assumption noted above: “non‑permanent spells” = instant/sorcery spells on the stack; if you meant something else (for example, modal spells or objects that aren’t instants/sorceries), say so and I’ll apply the appropriate rules.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text:
Yes. While a spell with split second is on the stack you may activate mana abilities, but you can’t cast other spells or activate non‑mana abilities.

Definition: A “mana ability” is one of the game’s activated or triggered abilities that meet the mana‑ability criteria (see rule 605.1) and are subject to special rules for mana abilities (see rule 113.4).

Why: Split second says that while the split second spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities, and that players may activate mana abilities and take special actions (rules 702.61a and 702.61b). Mana abilities don’t use the stack and resolve immediately (rules 113.4, 605.3b, 405.6c). Triggered mana abilities also resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them (rule 605.4a). You may only activate a mana ability when the game’s timing rules allow it (for example, when you have priority, or in the special cases described in rule 605.3a), and you can’t activate a mana ability if you can’t pay its costs (rule 117.1d and 118.3c). If an effect being resolved asks you to pay mana or allows casting during resolution, you may activate mana abilities as allowed by rule 608.2g and 605.3a.

Assumptions and scope: This answer uses only the provided rules. The outcome is the same in two‑player and multiplayer games under the provided rules (no multiplayer exception in the given text).

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first; when it resolves it counters Divination, so Divination is removed from the stack and does not resolve. 

Reasoning and definitions (assumptions below):
- When all players pass in succession, the top object on the stack resolves (see rules 608.1, 405.5, and 117.4). Therefore Counterspell, being on top of the stack, resolves first. 
- To “counter” a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack; it doesn’t resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard (see rule 701.6a). Counterspell’s text is “Counter target spell,” so when Counterspell resolves it cancels the targeted Divination and Divination is removed from the stack rather than resolving (see the card Counterspell and rule 701.6a). 
- As part of resolving an instant spell, the spell’s final step is putting that instant into its owner’s graveyard (see rule 608.2n); Counterspell itself is therefore put into its owner’s graveyard after it resolves. 
- A “spell” in this context is a card on the stack (see rule 112.1). 

Assumption and alternative timing: I’m assuming Divination remained a legal target for Counterspell at the moment Counterspell began to resolve. If Divination had become an illegal target before Counterspell resolved, Counterspell would not resolve (see rule 608.2b), and then Divination could remain on the stack to resolve later once it’s topmost and players pass.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You need to assign 1 damage from Charging Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk; the remaining 3 damage may be assigned to the defending player. Reasoning: Trample requires the attacking creature’s controller to assign lethal damage to blocking creatures before assigning any excess to the player (see 702.19b). Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of damage a source with deathtouch assigns to a creature is considered lethal for the purpose of determining excess damage (see 702.2c). Charging Rhino is a 4/4, and Vampire Nighthawk’s deathtouch makes 1 damage sufficient to be “lethal” for assignment, so you can assign 1 to Vampire Nighthawk and the other 3 to the player, assuming Vampire Nighthawk has no damage already marked on it and no other creatures are assigning damage this combat. If other creatures are assigning damage to Vampire Nighthawk during the same combat damage step, that damage is taken into account when determining whether lethal damage has been assigned (see 702.19b).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess will trigger when you cast the cascaded spell and that triggered ability will resolve before the cascaded spell resolves. Reasoning: Prowess is a triggered ability that says “Whenever you cast a noncreature spell, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn” [702.108a]. Shardless Agent’s cascade ability triggers when you cast Shardless Agent and resolves before Shardless Agent, and if you cast the exiled card it’s put onto the stack above Shardless Agent [Shardless Agent ruling #1]. When you cast that exiled noncreature spell, Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess triggers at the moment of casting [601.2i], and Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess trigger goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger and therefore resolves before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. Note also that once Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess has triggered it isn’t tied to the spell that caused it, so the prowess trigger will still resolve even if the cascaded spell is later countered [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #3]. Assumption: I’m assuming the card you cast via cascade is a noncreature spell (cascade can exile creature or noncreature cards; if the exiled card is a creature, Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess would not trigger).

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text:
Yes. Because Grizzly Bears already has damage equal to its toughness, state-based actions will destroy Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves.

Reasoning: State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and they don’t use the stack (704.1). They are performed each time a player would get priority, before that player receives priority (117.5). Damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step (120.6), and if the total damage marked on a creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action (302.7). Thus, with 2 damage already marked on Grizzly Bears (a 2/2), the state-based action that destroys it will be performed while Lightning Bolt is on the stack but before Lightning Bolt resolves. Note that damage itself doesn’t “destroy” the creature; the game’s state-based actions do that (120.5).

Assumptions and timing note: I’m assuming Lightning Bolt is on the stack and has not begun resolving yet, and this is the ordinary two-player timing sequence. If the damage were being created during the resolution of a spell or ability (instead of already being marked before resolution), state-based actions don’t “watch” intermediate changes during resolution in the same way (704.4), so the result could differ in that narrow case.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: Both triggered abilities trigger as the upkeep begins and are put onto the stack before either player receives priority. You (the active player) put any triggered abilities you control — including Phyrexian Arena’s “At the beginning of your upkeep…” trigger — onto the stack first in any order you choose; then your opponent (the nonactive player) puts any triggered abilities they control onto the stack in any order they choose. Because objects put onto the stack later become the topmost objects, your opponent’s upkeep trigger will end up on top of the stack and will resolve before Phyrexian Arena’s trigger.

Definitions and timing/assumptions: 
- A “triggered ability” is an ability written in the form “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition], [effect].” (Definition: [603.1].) 
- When the upkeep step begins, abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” that step trigger (that is, they notice the event and become triggered). Those triggered abilities are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority (upkeep abilities are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority). (See: [500.6], [603.2b], [503.1a], [117.3a].) 
- How multiple triggered abilities are placed on the stack: each player, in APNAP order, puts the triggered abilities they control onto the stack in any order they choose; the active player’s abilities are put on first, then nonactive players’ abilities. (See: [603.3b].) 
- Optional triggered abilities (those that say “may”) still go on the stack when they trigger; the controller’s choice is made when the ability resolves. (See: [603.5].)

Assumptions and multiplayer note: 
- I assumed you meant an opponent-controlled ability that actually triggers on your upkeep (for example, a permanent that says “At the beginning of each player’s upkeep …”); if the opponent’s ability only triggers on their own upkeep (worded “At the beginning of your upkeep …” and tied to their turn), it would not trigger on your upkeep and wouldn’t be involved. I also assumed a two-player game; in multiplayer or team games, triggered-ability placement follows team/APNAP rules (see [805.7] and [805.4d]) rather than the simple two-player APNAP ordering.

Practical result to act on: wait while both upkeep triggers are placed onto the stack before you get priority; your opponent’s upkeep-triggered ability will resolve first, then Phyrexian Arena’s ability will resolve.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
You get one copy of the card back in your hand: the original sorcery card returns to your hand because you paid its buyback cost; the copy created by Fork does not return anything. 

Reasoning and definitions
- Buyback: “Buyback [cost]” means “You may pay an additional [cost] as you cast this spell” and “If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves.” (See [702.27a].) You stated you paid the buyback when casting the sorcery, so as that spell (the actual card) resolves it is put into your hand instead of your graveyard. 
- Copy of a spell: To copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t a card and isn’t cast. A copy copies the characteristics and decisions made for the original, but it has no card associated with it. (See [707.10].) 
- Fork interaction: Fork puts a copy of the targeted instant or sorcery onto the stack; that copy has no card associated with it and therefore can’t be returned by buyback. The official ruling for Fork explicitly states: “If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you.” (See [Fork ruling #8] and [Fork ruling #10].)

Assumptions
- I assume the sorcery with buyback was cast from your hand (you said you paid buyback as you cast it). If you had cast it from a zone where buyback does not function differently, the provided buyback rule still governs the outcome.
- This outcome is the same in multiplayer and two-player games under the provided rules.

Short summary: the original sorcery card returns to your hand (1 card); the Fork-created copy does not return anything (0 cards).

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No — you do not get a token. Lightning Bolt is an instant card, and Mimic Vat ruling #0 says that if the creature that died was an instant or sorcery card that had been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled and you can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card; in that case no token is created. Assuming you exiled the face-down manifested Lightning Bolt with Mimic Vat and it remains exiled, activating Mimic Vat’s {3}, {T} ability later will not produce a token.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes. If Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability is copied with Lithoform Engine so that two creatures are exiled, both of those creatures return when Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield.

Reasoning: "Linked abilities" are a pair where one ability causes actions (here, Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability exiling creature cards) and the other ability refers to those actions or objects; the referring ability only looks at objects exiled by that first ability (see [607.1] and [607.2a]). If the exiling ability is copied, the copy is also linked to Fiend Hunter’s leave-the-battlefield ability, so the leave-the-battlefield ability refers to every card exiled by the original ability and the copy ([Lithoform Engine ruling #4]; see also [607.3]). Therefore, when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its leave-the-battlefield ability returns each card that was exiled by its enters-the-battlefield ability and the copy created by Lithoform Engine (both cards return) ([Lithoform Engine ruling #4]; [607.3]; [406.6]).

Assumption and alternate timing: I assumed Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield after the original and the copied enters-the-battlefield abilities have resolved and both creatures are exiled. If instead Fiend Hunter left the battlefield before its enters-the-battlefield ability (and the copied ability) resolved, then Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability would trigger and do nothing when it resolves; the later-resolution enter-the-battlefield ability and its copy would then exile the target(s) indefinitely (see [Fiend Hunter ruling #0]).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No — the exiled creature stays exiled; it does not return when Banishing Light phases out. Teferi's Protection's text and rulings make this specific. Teferi's Protection creates a phasing-out effect for your permanents, and Teferi's Protection ruling #21 states that “Any one-shot effects that are waiting 'until [this] leaves the battlefield,' such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out.” Phasing means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out and phasing in/out doesn't cause leaves-the-battlefield or enters-the-battlefield events to occur ([702.26d], [702.26c]; see also Teferi's Protection ruling #17). Therefore, because Banishing Light’s “until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield” delayed return is an effect that waits for Banishing Light to leave the battlefield, Banishing Light phasing out does not count as leaving the battlefield and so the exiled creature does not return.

Assumptions: I assume Teferi's Protection resolved and caused Banishing Light to phase out. If Banishing Light actually left the battlefield (for example, was destroyed or sacrificed) rather than phasing out, the creature would return because that would meet the “leaves the battlefield” condition.

This outcome is the same in two-player and multiplayer games for the situation you described (no player-leaves-the-game complications).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Short answer: Yes — your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell successfully counters Emrakul, the triggered ability created when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End still resolves (so you will gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn and that player will get the extra turn). 

Why: “Protection from instants” normally prevents being targeted by instants, but protection abilities apply only while the object with the ability is on the battlefield ([702.16b]; Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2). Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack while it’s a spell, so protection from instants does not stop an instant such as Counterspell from targeting the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2; Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1 clarifies what “protection from instants” prevents when Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield). 

When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End its triggered ability (“When you cast this spell, …”) triggers and is put on the stack as a triggered ability ([603.1a]). That triggered ability exists separately on the stack even if the Emrakul, the Promised End spell is later countered. When Counterspell resolves and successfully counters the Emrakul, the Promised End spell, the triggered ability you already created remains on the stack; when that triggered ability later resolves it checks whether its target is still legal and then does its effect. If you targeted the opponent with that triggered ability when it was created and that opponent is still a legal target (players don’t become illegal targets simply because the source spell was countered), the ability will resolve and you will gain control of target opponent during that player’s next turn and that player will take an extra turn afterward ([608.2b]; [608.2n]; [113.9]; Emrakul, the Promised End). 

Assumptions made: two-player game; you chose a target opponent for Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability when the ability was put on the stack. If you didn’t choose a legal target when the triggered ability was created, the ability would be removed when it checked targets on resolution ([603.1a]; [608.2b]). If multiple effects try to make players take or control turns, remember the most recently created applicable player-control effect is the one that works (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14).

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor can be the nonland card cascade stops on, and you may cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (the back face) without paying its mana cost, provided your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2. 

Why: Cascade exiles cards until it exiles a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value, then lets you cast that card without paying its mana cost (you take the casting action allowed by cascade) [702.85a]. Cards exiled by cascade are exiled face up so you can see the card and act on it [406.3b]. The modal double-faced card Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has a mana value of 2 (card data), so it is a legal hit for any cascade spell with mana value greater than 2. If you choose to cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, you may do so because an effect that lets you play or cast a card from a group of cards may let you play or cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits that effect’s criteria (here, the “resulting spell’s mana value is less than this spell’s mana value”) [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]. Remember that only the face you will put on the stack is evaluated when determining whether you can cast that face [712.11c], and under these rules the back-face cast in this situation meets the cascade criterion because the card’s mana value is 2 (which is less than your cascade spell’s mana value). 

Assumptions: I assume your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2 (if it isn’t, Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor would not be a legal hit). If your cascade spell’s mana value is 2 or less, the modal double-faced card would not satisfy the cascade mana-value test and wouldn’t be a hit.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You’ll end up controlling only one of the targeted player’s turns (their next turn), you will get a second Emrakul token when the copied Emrakul, the Promised End spell resolves, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not create another “When you cast this spell…” trigger.

Why: • A “copy” means putting a copy of a spell or ability onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an ability is itself an ability (707.10). • You copied the “When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End …” triggered ability with Lithoform Engine, so you have two instances of that triggered ability on the stack; each copied/resolving triggered ability will create its effects when it resolves (603.7h, 707.10). • Each resolving instance will create the control-effect for the targeted player’s next turn and will create an extra turn for that player after that turn. Multiple player‑controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other, and the last one created is the one that actually grants control (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14). In your sequence the copy-of-the-trigger resolves first and creates a control effect, then the original trigger resolves and creates a later control effect that overwrites the earlier one; net result: only the last-created control effect governs, so you control one of that player’s turns (their next turn). • Both resolved triggered abilities still create an extra turn each, so two extra turns will be created for that player; multiple extra turns are added one at a time and the most recently created extra turn is taken first (500.7, Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14). • When you use Lithoform Engine to copy Emrakul, the Promised End as a permanent spell, the copy is created on the stack and, as it resolves, becomes a token permanent (111.13; Lithoform Engine ruling #5). Because that copy was not cast, creating the copy won’t cause “when you cast this spell” triggers (Lithoform Engine ruling #6 and 707.10). Therefore the copied Emrakul, the Promised End becomes a second Emrakul token on the battlefield but does not produce an additional “When you cast this spell…” trigger.

Assumptions: two-player game; the described order is the actual order you performed the actions (you copied the triggered ability while the original trigger was on the stack, then later copied the permanent spell). If the order of resolving those two triggered abilities were changed, the “last-created” control effect would instead be whichever control effect is created last (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14).

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes — you get two tokens: one from Mimic Vat’s activated ability when it resolves and one from the copy of that activated ability created by Lithoform Engine when the copy resolves.

Why: copying an activated ability puts a copy of that ability onto the stack (a copy of an ability is itself an ability on the stack), so Lithoform Engine’s ability creates a second instance of Mimic Vat’s activated ability on the stack [707.10e, 707.10b; Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. A copy of an ability has the same source as the original ability, so both the original ability and the Lithoform Engine–created copy will refer to the same Mimic Vat when they resolve [707.10b; Lithoform Engine ruling #0]. Each ability, when it resolves, performs its instruction to create a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat, so each resolution creates its own token (and each token will be a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time that particular ability resolves) [Mimic Vat ruling #4].

Assumptions and notes: I assume there is at least one card exiled with Mimic Vat when these abilities resolve; if no card is exiled with Mimic Vat when an instance of the ability resolves, that instance creates no token (you may activate the ability with no card exiled, but if none is exiled by resolution nothing is created) [Mimic Vat ruling #6]. If the card exiled with Mimic Vat changes between the two abilities resolving, each ability will make a token copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at that ability’s resolution (they can therefore produce tokens of different cards) [Mimic Vat ruling #4].

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
Direct answer: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X = 0, you must pay a total of {1}{G}{G} (three mana: one of any color or colorless plus two green) and you create 0 tokens. To get tokens for that same locked-in total cost, choose X = 2 (that will create two 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens and lock in a total cost of {1}{G}{G}).

Reasoning and assumptions (short):
- Key term: X is the variable in Awaken the Woods’s mana cost {X}{G}{G}; when you cast a spell with an {X} in its mana cost you announce the value of X as part of casting it (see 107.3a and 601.2b). 
- Step-by-step for X = 0: Awaken the Woods’s announced mana cost is {0}{G}{G} (i.e. {G}{G}). Determine the total cost by adding increases and subtracting reductions, then apply Trinisphere’s effect last (per 601.2f and Trinisphere ruling #0). I assume the opponent’s Trinisphere is untapped and active (as you stated), and I assume your cost-reduction permanent reduces the spell’s generic portion only (the question’s wording implies “green spells cost {1} less”; I state this as an assumption because the numbered rules given don’t explicitly limit what a specific cost-reduction effect can reduce). Under that assumption, with X = 0 there is no generic portion to reduce, so after reductions the mana component is {G}{G} (two mana), which is less than three, so Trinisphere makes the spell cost three mana total. Restating the final locked-in total cost by symbol gives {1}{G}{G}. The spell’s effect “Create X 1/1 … tokens” creates X = 0 tokens.
- Why choose X = 2: If you announce X = 2, the printed mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. Apply your presumed −{1} generic reduction first (per 601.2f), leaving {1}{G}{G} (three total) before Trinisphere; because that mana component is already three, Trinisphere does not change it (Trinisphere is only applied if the mana component would be less than three, per Trinisphere ruling #0). The locked-in total cost is therefore {1}{G}{G}, and you get two tokens (X = 2). Choosing X = 1 or X = 0 both end up locked at {1}{G}{G} but produce only one or zero tokens respectively, so X = 2 is the smallest X that gives you tokens without increasing the locked-in total cost above three.

If you wanted more than two tokens, you can choose a larger X, but you’ll pay more mana: e.g. X = 3 (announced cost {3}{G}{G}) becomes {2}{G}{G} after your −{1} generic reduction (four total) and Trinisphere won’t increase it further.

If any assumption above is wrong (for example, your cost reducer can lower colored symbols rather than only the generic portion, or Trinisphere is tapped), the numeric outcomes change; say which assumption differs and I’ll recompute.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes. You can target and return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead, because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it's in any zone other than the battlefield [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1] and Animate Dead targets a creature card in a graveyard when cast [Animate Dead ruling #1]. However, when Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield it is no longer a creature and is just a planeswalker [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]. Animate Dead’s entering ability tries to make the Aura “enchant the creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura” and attach to that creature; because Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature after it enters, Animate Dead can’t legally be attached to it. In that case Animate Dead won’t be able to attach and will be put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action, which creates the delayed trigger that causes the returned permanent to be sacrificed if it’s still on the battlefield [Animate Dead ruling #4]. (This all assumes Animate Dead resolves and is on the battlefield as its enter-trigger resolves; if Animate Dead isn’t on the battlefield when that triggered ability would resolve, none of those effects happen and the creature card isn’t returned [Animate Dead ruling #0].)

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when you move it to the command zone, and it will enter the battlefield with those same four +1/+1 counters when you recast it. Doubling Season does not double those counters as Skullbriar re-enters.

Why: Normally an object that moves zones becomes a new object and counters don’t carry over ([400.7], [122.2]). However, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s oracle text explicitly says “Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library,” so Skullbriar keeps its counters while in the command zone (this is the card’s effect and is the controlling instruction for Skullbriar). Also, Skullbriar’s ruling #1 confirms it retains all its counters, and ruling #2 explains that those counters that “remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones” aren’t counters that are being “placed” on Skullbriar by an effect. Because Doubling Season only modifies effects that put counters onto permanents (and Doubling Season specifically affects counters that are placed when a permanent enters the battlefield, per Doubling Season ruling #2 and its card text), it doesn’t affect counters that merely remained on Skullbriar as it changed zones. Finally, moving Skullbriar from the graveyard to the command zone is permitted in Commander as a state-based option (you may put it into the command zone when it was put into the graveyard) ([903.9a]), which is the action you described.

Assumptions: I assume you moved Skullbriar, the Walking Grave to the command zone using the Commander rule after it died, then later cast it normally. If you instead did some different zone sequence not described here, the outcome could differ.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No — you don’t lose the game during that extra turn. Activating Sundial of the Infinite to “end the turn” before that turn’s end step causes the end step to be skipped and prevents any “at the beginning of the end step” triggers from triggering that turn; Sundial of the Infinite’s ruling says those abilities will instead trigger at the beginning of the next turn’s end step, so the Final Fortune triggered loss is delayed until that later end step unless something else prevents it. Definition: To “end the turn” as the result of an effect is to perform an expedited process that skips most things that would otherwise happen that turn (see rule 724). Assumption: this answer applies the ordinary rules for extra turns (two-player or multiplayer — the outcome is the same here).

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: Direct answer: You make Clone’s choice as Clone enters the battlefield — not while casting it. The controller of Clone chooses a creature already on the battlefield (you may also choose not to copy anything). Your opponent can’t respond to that choice itself; they can only respond to the Clone spell while it’s on the stack before it resolves (for example, by countering the spell).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total — one from the original Flooded Strand activation and two more from the two copies Gogo, Master of Mimicry creates.

Why: Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability (with X = 2) targets the activated ability of Flooded Strand that’s on the stack and “creates one or more additional instances of that ability on the stack” (so you end up with the original Flooded Strand ability plus two copies) [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. A copy of an activated ability is put onto the stack and is a copy of that ability; copies copy the characteristics and decisions of the original ability and have the same source as the original ability (so each copy is an instance of Flooded Strand’s ability and refers to Flooded Strand as its source) [707.10b], [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9].

Because the sacrifice of Flooded Strand was paid as part of activating the original ability, the copies are still valid instances on the stack and each resolving instance (the two copies and the original) will perform the ability’s effect (search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle). 707.10b explains that a copy uses the objects used to pay the original ability’s costs if the effect refers to those objects; Flooded Strand’s effect itself doesn’t require the source to be on the battlefield to put the searched land onto the battlefield, so each instance resolves and results in one land entering the battlefield [707.10b].

Assumptions: I assume you activated Flooded Strand first, then activated Gogo, Master of Mimicry while that Flooded Strand activated ability was on the stack, and Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability resolved before the original Flooded Strand ability (the usual timing for the scenario described). If instead the Flooded Strand ability had already resolved before Gogo targeted it (so it was no longer on the stack), Gogo couldn’t target it and no copies would be created. The outcome is the same in multiplayer and two-player games under these assumptions.
